en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 35: The Shorter Discourse to Saccaka (Cūḷasaccakasutta)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
Now at that time Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son was residing at Vesālī, a debater who prided himself on his learning and was esteemed as a wise man by many people.
He spoke these words in the assembly at Vesālī:
“I do not see any ascetic or brahmin— whether leader of a community, leader of a group, or teacher of a group—
even one who claims to be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, who, when engaged in debate with me,
would not tremble, shake, or shiver, nor from whose armpits sweat would break out.”
“If I were to engage in a debate with even an insentient pillar, it too would tremble, shake, and quiver when challenged by me in debate.
What need is there to speak of a human being?
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Assaji dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms.
While walking and wandering for exercise in Vesālī, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta saw the Venerable Assaji coming from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Venerable Assaji; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Assaji.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta said this to the Venerable Assaji:
“But how, Master Assaji, does the ascetic Gotama train his disciples, and what kind of instruction is frequently given by the ascetic Gotama to his disciples?
“It is in this way, Aggivessana, that the Blessed One trains his disciples, and it is this kind of instruction that is frequently given by the Blessed One to his disciples:
‘Bhikkhus, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent.’”
“Form, bhikkhus, is non-self; feeling is non-self; perception is non-self; volitional formations are non-self; consciousness is non-self. All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are non-self.
It is in this way, Aggivessana, that the Blessed One trains his disciples, and it is in this manner that the Blessed One’s instruction is frequently given to his disciples.
“Alas, Master Assaji, we have heard what should not have been heard, in that we have heard of the ascetic Gotama speaking thus!
Perhaps at some time or other we might meet with that Master Gotama; perhaps there might be some exchange of conversation, and perhaps we might be led away from that evil position.
Now at that time, about five hundred Licchavis had gathered in the assembly hall for some business or other.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta approached those Licchavis; having approached them, he said this to the Licchavis:
"Come forward, worthy Licchavis, come forward! Today I shall have a discussion and debate with the ascetic Gotama.
If the ascetic Gotama establishes himself in the same way that my disciple Assaji of the Ñātika clan has done..."
"Indeed, it has been established by the bhikkhu that just as a strong man might seize a long-haired sheep by its wool and drag it,
pull it, and drag it all around, even so will I drag, pull, and drag all around the ascetic Gotama in debate."
"Just as a powerful liquor-distiller, having thrown a large liquor-sieve into a deep pool of water, might pull it, drag it about, and haul it around by its handle;
even so will I pull, drag about, and haul around the ascetic Gotama in debate.
Or just as a powerful gambler, having seized a hair by its tip, might shake it, shake it out, and thump it."
"In the very same way, I shall shake, shake off, and batter the ascetic Gotama with word against word.
Just as a sixty-year-old elephant, having plunged into a deep lotus pond, plays at the game called 'the hemp-washer,' even so shall I play at the game of 'the hemp-washer' with the ascetic Gotama."
“Come forward, worthy Licchavis! Come forward, worthy Licchavis! Today I shall have a conversation and discussion with the ascetic Gotama.
Thereupon, some of the Licchavis said this:
“Will the ascetic Gotama refute the doctrine of Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, or will Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama?”
Some Licchavis said this:
"Who is this venerable Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta who will refute the Blessed One’s argument? Rather, it is the Blessed One who will refute the argument of Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta, surrounded by about five hundred Licchavis, approached the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were walking back and forth in the open air.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to them:
“Where, sirs, does the venerable Gotama dwell at present?”
“Indeed, we wish to see you, Master Gotama.
“This Blessed One, Aggivessana, has entered deep into the Great Wood and is seated at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.

Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta, together with a large assembly of Licchavis, entered deep into the Great Wood and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side.
Some of those Licchavis also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side;
others exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side.
They sat down. Some, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some, having announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.
Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son said this to the Blessed One:
“I would ask Master Gotama about a certain point, if Master Gotama would grant me the opportunity for an answer to my question.
“Ask, Aggivessana, whatever you wish.
“But how, Master Gotama, does Master Gotama train his disciples? And what kind of instruction is most frequently put into practice among Master Gotama’s disciples?”
“In this way, Aggivessana, I train my disciples, and such instruction is frequently given by me among my disciples:
‘Bhikkhus, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent;
consciousness is impermanent. Bhikkhus, form is non-self; feeling is non-self; perception is non-self; volitional formations are non-self; consciousness is non-self.’”
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all things are non-self.
It is in this way, Aggivessana, that I train my disciples, and it is in this manner that much of my instruction among my disciples proceeds.
“A simile occurs to me, Master Gotama,” he said.
“Let it occur to you, Aggivessana,” the Blessed One said.
“Just as, Master Gotama, whatever these plants and seeds that attain growth, increase, and abundance do so all by depending on the earth, established upon the earth;
even so do these plants and seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance.”
Or again, Master Gotama, just as whatever laborious tasks are performed, they are all done depending on the earth and established upon the earth;
it is thus that these laborious tasks are performed.
Even so, Master Gotama, this person, by means of form, established upon form, performs either merit or demerit.
Or, by way of feeling, this person, being established in feeling, produces merit or demerit;
by way of perception, this person, being established in perception, produces merit or demerit;
by way of volitional formations, this person, being established in volitional formations, produces merit or demerit.
“Because of consciousness, this person, having established themselves in consciousness, produces merit or demerit.
“But, Aggivessana, do you not say:
‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, volitional formations are my self, consciousness is my self’?”
“Master Gotama, I indeed say this:
‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, volitional formations are my self, consciousness is my self’—and so too does this great multitude.
“But what, Aggivessana, will a great multitude do for you? What can a great multitude possibly accomplish?”
“Come now, Aggivessana, unravel your own doctrine.
“I do indeed say this, Master Gotama:
‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, volitional formations are my self, consciousness is my self.’”
“In that case, Aggivessana, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.
What do you think, Aggivessana?
Would a head-anointed kṣatriya king exercise authority over his own realm?”
“Would he have the power to have this man executed, or to have him fined, or to have him banished, just as King Pasenadi of Kosala has, or as King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha has?
“He would have such power, Master Gotama; for a consecrated Kṣatriya king has authority over his own realm.”

"He may be killed, or he may be caused to be killed; he may be fined, or he may be caused to be fined; he may be banished, or he may be caused to be banished—just as in the case of King Pasenadi of Kosala, or indeed in the case of King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.
For even among these assemblies and groups, such as the Vajjis and the Mallas—"
Authority prevails within one’s own domain:
he who has the power to kill may kill, he who has the power to fine may fine, and he who has the power to banish may banish.
How much more so, then, for a head-anointed Khattiya king, such as King Pasenadi of Kosala, or indeed King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha?
“Venerable Gotama, he should conduct himself thus, and he is worthy to do so.
“What do you think, Aggivessana,
regarding what you have said?”
“‘Form is my self,’ do you have control over that form—to say, ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus’?
When this was said, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta became silent.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta:
"What do you think, Aggivessana?
Regarding what you say, 'Form is my self,' do you have control over that form?"
"May my form be thus; may my form not be thus"?
For a second time, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta remained silent.
Then the Blessed One said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta:

“Give an answer now, Aggivessana; this is no longer the time for silence. Aggivessana, if anyone does not answer a question put to them by the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dhamma up to three times, their head shall split into seven pieces right there. Now at that time, the yakkha Vajirapāṇi stood above Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta in the air, holding an iron thunderbolt that was blazing, glowing, and aflame, thinking: “If this Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta does not answer a question put to him by the Blessed One in accordance with the Dhamma up to three times, I will split his head into seven pieces with this iron thunderbolt. But the Blessed One saw the yakkha Vajirapāṇi standing there, and he said to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta: “Answer, Aggivessana; do not remain silent. If you do not answer a question put to you by the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dhamma up to three times, your head will split into seven pieces right here. “I am not afraid, O Blessed One, nor am I terrified. Let the Blessed One ask whatever he wishes. Then the Blessed One asked Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta: “Aggivessana, do you assert that the wind element is the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is the fire element the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is the water element the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is the earth element the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is form the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is feeling the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is perception the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Are volitional formations the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is consciousness the Tathāgata? “No, Blessed One. “Is it in form that the Tathāgata exists? “No, Blessed One. “Is it in feeling that the Tathāgata exists? “No, Blessed One. “Is it in perception that the Tathāgata exists? “No, Blessed One. “Is it in volitional formations that the Tathāgata exists? “No, Blessed One. “Is it in consciousness that the Tathāgata exists? “No, Blessed One. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from form? “No, Blessed One. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from feeling? “No, Blessed One. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from perception? “No, Blessed One. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from volitional formations? “No, Blessed One. “Does the Tathāgata exist apart from consciousness? “No, Blessed One. “Then, Aggivessana, the Tathāgata does not exist at all? “No, Blessed One. “Aggivessana, when you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata the wind element? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata the fire element? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata the water element? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata the earth element? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata form? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata feeling? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata perception? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Are the Tathāgata’s volitional formations? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Is the Tathāgata consciousness? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist in form? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist in feeling? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist in perception? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist in volitional formations? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist in consciousness? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from form? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from feeling? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from perception? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from volitional formations? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata exist apart from consciousness? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. When you are asked: ‘Then, Aggivessana, the Tathāgata does not exist at all? you say, ‘No, Blessed One. So, Aggivessana, since you cannot find the Tathāgata anywhere, what is it that you praise? What is it that you hold up as a standard? Who is it that you revile? “Blessed One, I do not praise anything, nor do I hold up anything as a standard, nor do I revile anyone. “But, Aggivessana, when you do not praise anything, nor hold up anything as a standard, nor revile anyone, why do you go about with such a loud voice, making such a great noise, shouting: ‘There is nothing to be grasped at, there is nothing to be grasped at’? “Blessed One, I do not go about with a loud voice, nor do I make a great noise, nor do I shout: ‘There is nothing to be grasped at, there is nothing to be grasped at. Rather, Blessed One, I go about in silence, having seen that there is nothing to be grasped at. “But, Aggivessana, who has taught you this doctrine? “The venerable Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Blessed One. “What does the venerable Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta teach, Aggivessana? “The venerable Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta teaches thus, Blessed One: ‘If one is asked: “Is there a world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is a world beyond”; and if one is asked: “Is there no world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is no world beyond. If one is asked: “Does the world beyond exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond exists”; and if one is asked: “Does the world beyond not exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond does not exist. If one is asked: “Is there a world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is a world beyond”; and if one is asked: “Is there no world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is no world beyond. If one is asked: “Does the world beyond exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond exists”; and if one is asked: “Does the world beyond not exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond does not exist. If one is asked: “Is there a world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is a world beyond”; and if one is asked: “Is there no world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is no world beyond. If one is asked: “Does the world beyond exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond exists”; and if one is asked: “Does the world beyond not exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond does not exist. If one is asked: “Is there a world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is a world beyond”; and if one is asked: “Is there no world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is no world beyond. If one is asked: “Does the world beyond exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond exists”; and if one is asked: “Does the world beyond not exist? one should say: “It is not the case that the world beyond does not exist. If one is asked: “Is there a world beyond? one should say: “It is not the case that there is a world beyond”; and if one is asked: “Is there no world
“If this Saccaka, son of the Nigaṇṭhas, does not answer a question consistent with the Dhamma when asked for a third time by the Blessed One, I shall split his head into seven pieces right here!
Now, both the Blessed One and Saccaka, son of the Nigaṇṭhas, saw that yakkha Vajirapāṇi.

Then Saccaka, son of the Nigaṇṭhas, terrified, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, sought refuge in the Blessed One alone, sought shelter in the Blessed One alone, and sought protection in the Blessed One alone; he then said this to the Blessed One:
“Let Master Gotama question me; I shall answer.
“What do you think, Aggivessana, regarding this which you say:”
“If one says, ‘Form is my self,’ do you have control over that form—to say, ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“Pay attention, Aggivessana;
having paid attention, Aggivessana, give your answer.
What you have said does not connect with what preceded it, nor does what followed it connect with what preceded it.”
What do you think, Aggivessana?
When you say,
“Feeling is my self,” do you have control over that feeling?
“‘May my feeling be thus; may my feeling not be thus’?”—
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”—
“Pay attention, Aggivessana.”
"Having reflected upon it, Aggivessana, give your answer.
For what you say does not cohere with what precedes it, nor does what follows it cohere with what precedes it.
What do you think, Aggivessana?"
When you say, “Perception is my self,” do you have control over that perception such that you can say:
“Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be thus”?
“No, Master Gotama.
“Pay attention, Aggivessana;
having paid attention, Aggivessana, give your answer.”
"Indeed, what you say does not cohere with what precedes it, nor does what follows it cohere with what precedes it.
What do you think, Aggivessana,
regarding this which you say?"
“‘Formations are my self’—do you have power over those formations such that you can say, ‘Let my formations be thus; let my formations not be thus’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“Pay attention, Aggivessana;
having paid attention, Aggivessana, give your answer.
For what you have said does not connect with what preceded it, nor does what follows it connect with what preceded it.”
What do you think, Aggivessana?
When you say,
“Consciousness is my self,” do you exercise control over that consciousness?
“‘May my consciousness be thus, may my consciousness not be thus’?”—
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”—
“Pay attention, Aggivessana.”
"Pay close attention, Aggivessana, and then answer.
What you have said does not cohere with what preceded it, nor does what follows cohere with what has gone before.
What do you think, Aggivessana?"
“Is form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Master Gotama.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, Master Gotama.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, Aggivessana,
is feeling … [and so on] …”
“Perception … formations … What do you think, Aggivessana, is consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, Master Gotama.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Master Gotama.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“What do you think, Aggivessana?
Suppose someone is attached to suffering, has approached suffering, and is obsessed with suffering, and regards suffering thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Would such a person, by himself, come to fully understand suffering?”
“Or having surrounded it, would he dwell [there]?
“What else could it be, Master Gotama?
Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“What do you think, Aggivessana, since this is so,
are you not clinging to suffering, approaching suffering, adhering to suffering,
and regarding suffering as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“What could it be for us, Master Gotama?
It is so, Master Gotama.
“Suppose, Aggivessana, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest.
Suppose he were to see there a large plantain trunk, straight, fresh, and not worm-eaten.
He would cut it down at the base; having cut it down at the base, he would cut off the top; having cut off the top, he would peel away the layers of the sheath.
While peeling away the layers of the sheath, he would not find even pith there, much less heartwood.
In the same way, Aggivessana, when you were cross-examined, interrogated, and rebuked by me regarding your own doctrine, you were found empty, hollow, and at fault.
Yet this speech was uttered by you, Aggivessana, in the assembly at Vesālī:
“I do not see any ascetic or brahmin—whether he be the head of an order, the head of a group, a teacher of a group, or even an Arhat—who could refute my statement.”
“Whoever claims to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha would not tremble, would not shake, and would not quiver when engaged in debate with me;
nor would sweat break out from his armpits.
Even if I were to engage a senseless pillar in debate, that pillar too, when engaged by me in debate, would tremble, would shake, and would quiver.”
"What need is there to speak of one who has become human?
"But, Aggivessana, some drops of sweat have even now fallen from your forehead, having broken through your upper robe and landed on the ground.
However, Aggivessana, there is at present no sweat in my body."
Thus the Blessed One revealed his golden-hued body to that assembly.
When this was said, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son sat silent, ashamed, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, brooding, and speechless.
Then Dummukha the Licchavi youth, seeing Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son thus silent, ashamed, with shoulders slumped, head bowed, brooding, and speechless, addressed the Blessed One:
“A simile occurs to me, Blessed One.
“Let it occur to you, Dummukha,” the Blessed One said.
“Just as if, venerable sir, there were a lotus pond not far from a village or a town.”
There he would have a crab.
Then, Bhante, many boys or girls might come out from that village or town and approach that lotus pond;
having approached and entered that lotus pond, they [would see] that...
Suppose they were to pull a crab out of the water and set it on dry land.
Whatever claw that crab might extend, those boys or girls would cut it off with a stick or a stone, break it, and crush it completely.
In this way, venerable sir, with all its claws cut off, broken, and crushed, that crab would be unable to enter that lotus pond again, just as it was before.
“In the same way, venerable sir, all those deceptions, maneuvers, and writhings of Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son have been cut down, broken, and shattered by the Blessed One.
And now, venerable sir, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son is incapable of approaching the Blessed One again with the intention of debate.
When this was said, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son said this to Dummukha the Licchavi:
“Wait, Dummukha, wait, Dummukha! (…) We do not consult with you; here we consult with Master Gotama. Let this talk of ours and that of other common recluses and brahmins stand aside.
I consider it mere idle chatter.”

“To what extent, Master Gotama, is one a disciple who acts according to the teaching, who responds to exhortation, who has crossed over doubt, who is free from perplexity, who has attained self-confidence, and who dwells in the Teacher’s dispensation independent of others?
“In this case, Aggivessana, my disciple regards whatever form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that [as it really is].”
One sees form as it really is with correct wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self”;
whatever feeling there is...
whatever perception there is... [and so on].
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is "not mine, this I am not."
‘This is not my self’—thus one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.

To this extent, Aggivessana, a disciple of mine is a doer of the Teacher’s bidding, a follower of his advice, one who has crossed beyond doubt, is free from perplexity, has attained intrepidity, and dwells independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation.

“But to what extent, Master Gotama, is a bhikkhu an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge?”
“Here, Aggivessana, a bhikkhu regards whatever form—whether past, future, or present;
internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form as:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus he sees it as it really is with correct wisdom.”
Having seen this, he becomes liberated through non-clinging;
whatever feeling there may be … whatever perception there may be … [and so on].
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is "not mine, this I am not."
‘This is not my self’—having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one is liberated through non-clinging.

To this extent, Aggivessana, a bhikkhu is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right gnosis.
With a mind thus liberated, Aggivessana, a bhikkhu is endowed with three unsurpassable qualities.
“By the unsurpassed vision, by the unsurpassed practice, and by the unsurpassed liberation.
Thus, Aggivessana, a bhikkhu whose mind is liberated honors, reveres, respects, and venerates only the Tathāgata:
‘That Blessed One is a Buddha; he teaches the Dhamma for awakening. That Blessed One is self-controlled; he teaches the Dhamma for self-control.’”
“The Blessed One is at peace; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of peace. The Blessed One has crossed over; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of crossing over.
The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of final Nibbāna.
When this was said, Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“We are indeed shameless, Master Gotama; we are impudent, we who thought it right to provoke Master Gotama with our arguments.
For it might be possible for a man to remain safe after attacking a rutting elephant, but it would not be possible for a man to remain safe after attacking Master Gotama.
For it might be possible for a man to remain safe after attacking a blazing mass of fire, but it would not be possible for a man to remain safe after attacking Master Gotama.”

"It might indeed be possible for a man to remain safe after attacking a fierce venomous snake, Master Gotama, but it would not be possible for a man to remain safe after attacking the venerable Gotama.
We alone, Master Gotama, are the shameless ones; we alone are the impudent ones, we who thought we could attack the venerable Gotama with word against word.
May the venerable Gotama, together with the community of monks, accept tomorrow’s meal from me."
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, addressed those Licchavis:
"Listen, worthy Licchavis, the ascetic Gotama has been invited by me for tomorrow’s meal, together with the community of monks."
"Therefore, you should bring me whatever you deem appropriate.
Then, at the end of that night, those Licchavis brought five hundred pots of cooked rice as a meal-offering for Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas.
Then the Nigaṇṭha’s son, having had choice hard and soft foods prepared in his own monastery, had the time announced to the Blessed One:
“It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the park of Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta, with his own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha-putta said this to the Blessed One:
"Whatever merit and great fruit there is, Master Gotama, in giving, may that lead to the happiness of the donors."
“Aggivessana, whatever merit comes from approaching such a worthy recipient who is not free from lust, hatred, and delusion, that will belong to the donors.
But whatever merit comes from approaching a worthy recipient like me, who is free from lust, hatred, and delusion, that will belong to you.
The Shorter Saccaka Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.
